raw_case_text:
A 19-year-old male was admitted to hospital with coughing and increasing shortness of breath over a duration of 4 days. He reported experiencing chest pain, discomfort, and a stabbing sensation in his chest. Figure 1 presents a timeline of the hospitalization, including test, examinations, and treatments.
The patient's vital signs upon examination revealed a blood pressure of 151/86 mmHg, a pulse rate of 134 bpm, a temperature of 37.7 C (measured by ear), a respiratory rate of 25 breaths per minute, and an oxygen saturation level of 88%.
Prior to commencing oxygen therapy, the patient's arterial blood gas analysis revealed the following values: pH = 7.4, PaCO2 = 5.8 kPa, PaO2 = 6.8 kPa, oxygen saturation = 85%, and bicarbonate = 26 mmol/L. Following the administration of oxygen therapy at a rate of 20 L/min, the patient's arterial blood gas parameters improved to pH = 7.36, PaCO2 = 6.5 kPa, PaO2 = 9.4 kPa, saturation = 93%, and bicarbonate = 25 mmol/L
The patient presented with a clean medical record devoid of prior medical conditions or pharmaceutical usage. Nevertheless, he reported smoking approximately 35 cigarettes a day, along with a recent yearlong usage of cannabis. Furthermore, in the week leading up to admission, the patient stated an extensive use of a vaping device filled with flavored liquids. The brand unknown and per the patient's report, without cannabinoids. He was subsequently admitted to the intensive care unit and expeditious intubated due to severe hypoxia.
Initial microbiological tests for the following were conducted: Covid-19, influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, atypical pneumonias, including mycoplasma pneumonia, legionella pneumophila, Chlamydophila pneumonia and Chlamydophila psittaci. Furthermore, blood cultures, urine cultures, sputum cultures and tracheal secretions were examined for cultivation and resistance.
The initial hematological analysis revealed an elevated number of total leukocytes (35.9 x 10^9/L), predominantly consisting of neutrophils (32.8 x 10^9/L). Additionally, inflammatory biomarkers were increased, with C-reactive protein levels registering at 200 mg/l initially, escalating to 380 mg/l after 3 days. Procalcitonin exhibited a markedly elevated level of 21 ng/ml. Lactate dehydrogenase levels were measured at 270 units/L. Despite the absence of a confirmed bacterial infection, preemptive treatment with piperacillin, tazobactam, and clarithromycin was initiated.
Notably, all the microbiological tests were conducted prior to the administration of antibiotics.
The bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was deemed too high risk due to the patient's high oxygen requirements.
Tracheal secretions for culture and resistance and inoculation for legionella were repeated.
Additionally, examination for Aspergillus fumigatus galactomannan in blood was negative.
After 2 days, the patient was referred to a tertiary hospital due to additional respiratory deterioration and the need for additional respiratory support in the form of extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).
A chest radiograph displayed bilateral diffuse patchy infiltrates and consolidations in the upper and lower lobes of the right lung, as seen in Figure 2. 
Additionally, a human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) test was conducted, yielding a negative result.
During bronchoscopy, minor mucosal bleeding was observed along with bilateral sporadic mucosal plugs in the distal segments, accompanied predominantly by scant secretion. Subsequently, BAL was meticulously analyzed, yielding negative results across all microbiological assessments, including those for Aspergillus galactomannan, tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, nocardia, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, Pneumocystis jirovecii, actinomyces, herpes simplex virus, and varicella-zoster. Additionally, analyses of bronchial lavage showed 75-80% neutrophils and 20-25% macrophages. There were very few lymphocytes and occasional eosinophils. No fungi, malignant cells, or recognizable viral changes were observed.
All of this corroborates the diagnosis of EVALI, given its classification as a diagnosis of exclusion.
A chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) and a cerebral CT scan were conducted on day 5 of admission. The cerebral CT scan showed no abnormalities. However, the chest HRCT revealed bilateral consolidations, notable consolidation in the lower lobes bilaterally, featuring visible air bronchograms, bilateral peribronchovascular infiltrates, and bilateral patchy infiltrates displaying diffuse ground glass opacities, as seen in Figure 3.
The pathologists suggested a range of diagnoses based on the BAL material. However, based on clinical and paraclinical data, as well as vital parameters, there were no signs of either acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), or acute eosinophilic pneumonia. The CT scan did not correlate with organizing pneumonia (OP). The most probable diagnosis was EVALI based on the patient's vaping history. However, ruling out lipoid pneumonia and peribronchial granulomatous pneumonitis was not feasible due to the impracticality of additional invasive diagnostic procedures such as surgical or bronchoscopic lung biopsy, which carried a high risk.
A transthoracic echocardiogram revealed a nearly normal left ventricular ejection fraction with minimal pericardial effusion. No dilation of the right vena cava or significant valve abnormalities were noted. Sinus tachycardia with a heart rate of 136 bpm was observed on the electrocardiogram (ECG) without evidence of ischemia. Renal function was within normal limits but exhibited slight fluctuations. Treatment was initiated with meropenem, fluconazole, acyclovir, azithromycin, and corticosteroids to ensure comprehensive coverage.
After 22 days of mechanical ventilation and 20 days on ECMO, attempts were made to discontinue ECMO, but were unsuccessful. It required an additional 18 days before successful weaning from ECMO was achieved and a total of 63 days on mechanical ventilation. Approximately 3 months and 2 weeks following hospitalization, the patient was discharged from the ICU and transferred to a local hospital to commence rehabilitation. Rehabilitation efforts continued after discharge, which occurred 2 weeks later due to the development of a fungal sepsis which was treated adequately.
Therefore, the patient was hospitalized for a total of approximately 3 months and 4 weeks before discharge.
The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation center. He underwent a two-month rehabilitation program before being discharged home. Two and a half months post-hospital discharge, the initial pulmonary function test revealed significantly reduced lung function, with FEV1 at 38% of predicted, FVC at 54%, and FEV1/FVC ratio at 60% of predicted. Subsequent pulmonary function test consistently demonstrated reduced lung function to varying degrees, as shown in Table 1. Despite strong advisement against it, the patient resumed smoking both cigarettes and E-cigarettes and continues to do so presently. 
Initially, the patient received prednisolone via nasogastric tube at a dose of 100 mg daily for 4 days, followed by a tapered regimen of oral prednisolone at 40 mg daily for 3 days, and subsequently, a tapering regimen of 5 mg oral prednisolone every third day was initiated. Corticosteroids have been documented to show efficacy in managing EVALI, potentially by reducing pulmonary inflammation. In a cohort of 140 cases admitted to the CDC, 82% of the patients demonstrated clinical improvement when treated with corticosteroids. Nevertheless, the natural course of this injury is unknown, and it is possible that patients may recover without corticosteroids or by discontinuing the use of vaping devices. In conditions where corticosteroids could exacerbate the patient's condition, such as fungal pneumonia, alternative treatment options should be carefully considered, and generally, the use of corticosteroids should be decided in consultation with a pulmonologist.
Additionally, in cases where mechanical ventilation is ineffective, ECMO should be considered. As illustrated in this case, the patient required both intubation and ECMO therapy for several weeks.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 19-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of cough, worsening shortness of breath, and stabbing chest pain.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the 4 days prior to admission, the patient developed progressive dyspnea, cough, chest discomfort, and a stabbing sensation in the chest, rapidly progressing to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring ICU admission and endotracheal intubation.
subjective.past_medical_history: No prior medical conditions or home medications. Social history was significant for smoking ~35 cigarettes/day, a 1-year history of cannabis use, and heavy use of a flavored e-cigarette/vaping device (reportedly cannabinoid-free) during the week prior to admission.

objective.physical_examination: On admission: BP 151/86 mmHg, pulse 134 bpm, ear temperature 37.7 C, respiratory rate 25 breaths/min, and SpO2 88% on room air.
objective.routine_investigations: Room air ABG: pH 7.4, PaCO2 5.8 kPa, PaO2 6.8 kPa, SaO2 85%, HCO3 26 mmol/L (improving on 20 L/min O2 to pH 7.36, PaCO2 6.5 kPa, PaO2 9.4 kPa, SaO2 93%, HCO3 25 mmol/L). Hematology showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 35.9 x 10^9/L, neutrophils 32.8 x 10^9/L), CRP 200 mg/L (rising to 380 mg/L on day 3), procalcitonin 21 ng/mL, and LDH 270 U/L; renal function was normal. Chest X-ray showed bilateral diffuse patchy infiltrates and right upper/lower lobe consolidations. ECG showed sinus tachycardia (136 bpm) without ischemia; TTE showed nearly normal LVEF with minimal pericardial effusion. HIV test, blood Aspergillus galactomannan, respiratory viral/atypical PCRs (SARS-CoV-2, influenza, RSV, Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydophila), and blood, urine, sputum, and tracheal cultures were all negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Bronchoscopy revealed minor mucosal bleeding and bilateral distal mucosal plugs with scant secretions; BAL cytology showed 75-80% neutrophils and 20-25% macrophages without fungi, viral inclusions, or malignancy, and extensive BAL microbiology (including Nocardia, Actinomyces, M. tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, Aspergillus galactomannan, P. jirovecii, CMV, EBV, HSV, VZV) was completely negative. Day-5 brain CT was normal; chest HRCT showed bilateral lower-lobe consolidations with air bronchograms, peribronchovascular infiltrates, and diffuse ground-glass opacities. Follow-up PFTs 2.5 months post-discharge showed severe restriction/obstruction (FEV1 38% predicted, FVC 54%, FEV1/FVC 60%).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: E-cigarette or vaping product use-associated lung injury (EVALI) was diagnosed by exclusion after comprehensive microbiological workup (including Nocardia, Actinomyces, fungal, mycobacterial, and viral testing) proved negative. Following empirical piperacillin-tazobactam, clarithromycin, meropenem, fluconazole, acyclovir, and azithromycin, he was treated with nasogastric prednisolone (100 mg daily for 4 days, 40 mg daily for 3 days, then tapered by 5 mg every 3 days) and prolonged mechanical ventilation (63 days total) plus veno-venous ECMO (38 days total). After nearly 4 months of hospitalization and 2 months of inpatient rehabilitation, he was discharged home with persistent pulmonary function impairment.
